President Obama’s hair is definitely grayer these days, and no doubt trying to manage foreign policy in a world of increasing disorder accounts for at least half of those gray hairs. (The Tea Party can claim the other half.) But having had a chance to spend an hour touring the horizon with him in the White House Map Room late Friday afternoon, it’s clear that the president has a take on the world, born of many lessons over the last six years, and he has feisty answers for all his foreign policy critics.
Obama made clear that he is only going to involve America more deeply in places like the Middle East to the extent that the different communities there agree to an inclusive politics of no victor/no vanquished. The United States is not going to be the air force of Iraqi Shiites or any other faction. Despite Western sanctions, he cautioned, President Vladimir Putin of Russia “could invade” Ukraine at any time, and, if he does, “trying to find our way back to a cooperative functioning relationship with Russia during the remainder of my term will be much more difficult.” Intervening in Libya to prevent a massacre was the right thing to do, Obama argued, but doing it without sufficient follow-up on the ground to manage Libya’s transition to more democratic politics is probably his biggest foreign policy regret.
At the end of the day, the president mused, the biggest threat to America — the only force that can really weaken us — is us. We have so many things going for us right now as a country — from new energy resources to innovation to a growing economy — but, he said, we will never realize our full potential unless our two parties adopt the same outlook that we’re asking of Shiites, Sunnis and Kurds or Israelis and Palestinians: No victor, no vanquished and work together.
“Our politics are dysfunctional,” said the president, and we should heed the terrible divisions in the Middle East as a “warning to us: societies don’t work if political factions take maximalist positions. And the more diverse the country is, the less it can afford to take maximalist positions.”
While he blamed the rise of the Republican far right for extinguishing so many potential compromises, Obama also acknowledged that gerrymandering, the Balkanization of the news media and uncontrolled money in politics — the guts of our political system today — are sapping our ability to face big challenges together, more than any foreign enemy. “Increasingly politicians are rewarded for taking the most extreme maximalist positions,” he said, “and sooner or later, that catches up with you.”
I began by asking whether if former Secretary of State Dean Acheson was “present at the creation” of the post-World War II order, as he once wrote, did Obama feel present at the “disintegration?”
“First of all, I think you can’t generalize across the globe because there are a bunch of places where good news keeps coming.” Look at Asia, he said, countries like Indonesia, and many countries in Latin America, like Chile. “But I do believe,” he added, “that what we’re seeing in the Middle East and parts of North Africa is an order that dates back to World War I starting to buckle.”

The fact is, said the president, in Iraq a residual U.S. troop presence would never have been needed had the Shiite majority there not “squandered an opportunity” to share power with Sunnis and Kurds. “Had the Shia majority seized the opportunity to reach out to the Sunnis and the Kurds in a more effective way, [and not] passed legislation like de-Baathification,” no outside troops would have been necessary. Absent their will to do that, our troops sooner or later would have been caught in the crossfire, he argued.
With “respect to Syria,” said the president, the notion that arming the rebels would have made a difference has “always been a fantasy. This idea that we could provide some light arms or even more sophisticated arms to what was essentially an opposition made up of former doctors, farmers, pharmacists and so forth, and that they were going to be able to battle not only a well-armed state but also a well-armed state backed by Russia, backed by Iran, a battle-hardened Hezbollah, that was never in the cards.”
Even now, the president said, the administration has difficulty finding, training and arming a sufficient cadre of secular Syrian rebels: “There’s not as much capacity as you would hope.”
The “broader point we need to stay focused on,” he added, “is what we have is a disaffected Sunni minority in the case of Iraq, a majority in the case of Syria, stretching from essentially Baghdad to Damascus. ... Unless we can give them a formula that speaks to the aspirations of that population, we are inevitably going to have problems. ... Unfortunately, there was a period of time where the Shia majority in Iraq didn’t fully understand that. They’re starting to understand it now. KABUL, Afghanistan — In one of the most significant coordinated assaults on the government in years, the Taliban have attacked police outposts and government facilities across several districts in northern Helmand Province, sending police and military officials scrambling to shore up defenses and heralding a troubling new chapter as coalition forces prepare to depart.
The attacks have focused on the district of Sangin, historically an insurgent stronghold and one of the deadliest districts in the country for the American and British forces who fought for years to secure it. The Taliban have mounted simultaneous attempts to conquer territory in the neighboring districts of Now Zad, Musa Qala and Kajaki. In the past week, more than 100 members of the Afghan forces and 50 civilians have been killed or wounded in fierce fighting, according to early estimates from local officials.
With a deepening
political crisis
in Kabul already casting the presidential election and long-term political stability into doubt, the Taliban offensive presents a new worst-case situation for Western officials: an aggressive insurgent push that is seizing territory even before American troops have completed their withdrawal from Afghanistan.
The battle in Helmand is playing out as, about 1,500 miles to the west, Iraq is losing ground to an insurgent force that advanced in the shadow of the American withdrawal there. The fear pulsing through Afghanistan is that it, too, could fall apart after the NATO-led military coalition departs in 2016.
Already, areas once heavily patrolled by American forces have grown more violent as the Afghan military and the police struggle to feed, fuel and equip themselves. The lackluster performance of the Afghan Army so far in Helmand has also evoked comparisons with Iraq, raising questions about whether the American-trained force can stand in the way of a Taliban resurgence.
Officials in Helmand say the answers may come soon enough.
“The Taliban are trying to overrun several districts of northern Helmand and find a permanent sanctuary for themselves,” said Hajji Mohammad Sharif, the district governor for Musa Qala. “From there, they pose threats to the southern parts of Helmand and also pose threats to Kandahar and Oruzgan Provinces.”

The Taliban have repeatedly used the area to make a statement about the limits of Afghan and Western government strength, and local officials fear a similar approach now.
“The Taliban are planning to create problems in several northern Helmand districts to pave the way for their fighters to operate freely in the area and pose threats to Kandahar, Helmand and Farah Provinces,” said Muhammad Naim Baloch, the provincial governor in Helmand.
Only now, the task to secure the district has fallen exclusively to the Afghans, and it is providing an early test of the forces the international coalition has spent years training to take over the fight.
Last summer in Sangin, Afghan forces
got their first taste
of what that fight would look like. Struggling to keep the Taliban at bay, they lost checkpoints, hard-fought ground and more than 120 men.
The government shuffled commanders, but it hardly mattered. By the end of the fighting season, the cowed Afghan Army unit there was mostly unwilling to leave its base to confront the threat. Late last year, reports of a deal between a local army commander and the Taliban began to surface, driven in part by attrition rates of nearly 50 percent and the near constant threat of death.
Given the debacle last summer, the military’s lack of preparedness so far this year is all the more striking. Police officers ran out of ammunition, and in some cases bodies could not be recovered because of the fighting. Even though Helmand is the only province with an entire corps dedicated to it, the army has struggled to defend it.
The fighting this summer appears to be worse. In just one week, the security forces appear to have sustained almost half the casualties they suffered in all of last summer, though reports differ on the exact toll.
Last Saturday, as many as 600 Taliban insurgents stormed checkpoints through portions of Sangin, claiming wide tracts of land. On Sunday, the militants attacked the neighboring district of Now Zad. Violence erupted in Musa Qala on Monday, when the Taliban again stormed police checkpoints but were prevented from reaching the district center.
The assault on Sangin seems the most concerted. On Friday night, according to the district governor, the Taliban advanced on the district center itself. The army repelled the attack through the district bazaar, while the police stopped an attempted breach from the north.

Though exact data is nearly impossible to obtain, in part because there is no longer a coalition footprint in the area, the extent of the attack offers a new perspective through which to view the Taliban’s ambitions, especially now that the militants no longer fear the dreaded American air support that has for years prevented them from massing in large groups.

Residents described a hellish scene for those trapped in the area. Some have started to question whether the fight, and its toll on the people, is even worth it.

RICHMOND, Va. —  Closing arguments in the corruption trial of former Gov.
Bob McDonnell
of Virginia and his wife, Maureen, are scheduled for Friday after 23 days of testimony that has often played as a soap opera and has drawn wide attention.
But on Thursday, the proceedings were drier as Judge James R. Spencer excused the jury early for a debate in Federal District Court between government and defense lawyers on the instructions that jurors will hear.
The McDonnells are accused of 14 counts of bribery, extortion and related crimes that could send the former governor, once a rising Republican star whom Mitt Romney considered for vice president, to prison for years.
On Thursday, each side tried to get the judge to cast his description of the law for jurors to benefit its case. But the debate was also a preview of closing arguments, and for the defense, a hint of grounds for an appeal in case of convictions.
The sides tangled especially over what is required
to prove bribery
. The McDonnells are charged with taking money and gifts from a Virginia businessman, Jonnie R. Williams Sr., in exchange for promoting his nutritional supplement business, including at two events at the Governor’s Mansion, and for setting up meetings for Mr. Williams with state officials.
Neither side disputes that the McDonnells received about $177,000 in luxury goods, cash and loans on favorable terms from Mr. Williams — not in itself illegal in Virginia.
The government argued it did not need to show Mr. McDonnell had accepted any particular gift in trade for a specific favor, only that he had been available to help Mr. Williams over time. “The jury needs to understand it’s not this Ferrari ride for this official meeting,” argued Ryan Faulconer, an assistant United States attorney.
A lawyer for Mr. McDonnell, Noel Francisco, strenuously disagreed, arguing that accepting a gift “for some unspecified future act” was not bribery. He asked the judge to tell the jury that.
The defense also wanted the judge to tell jurors that not all of Mr. McDonnell’s efforts for Mr. Williams had risen to the level of “official action,” which is necessary to convict him. “Things as innocuous as asking for a meeting” are not official acts, Mr. Francisco insisted.
The judge’s instructions will be given to the legal teams before closing arguments, and later to the jury.
Earlier in the day, when the jury heard from the trial’s last witness, the state of the McDonnells’ 38-year marriage was again the topic. They each are facing two counts of conspiracy. Their lawyers have argued that Mr. McDonnell, who once called protecting “the traditional family” the Republican “issue of the decade,” was all along in a sham marriage, in which he and his wife barely spoke.
An agent with the
F.B.I.
who analyzed the couple’s schedules for the prosecution testified that in the 24 months covered by the indictment, they spent a vast majority of nights under the same roof. The testimony, complete with pie charts, was meant to undermine defense claims that the McDonnells were estranged and in no position to conspire about anything.
According to the F.B.I. agent, Kathryn Weber, the McDonnells spent 644 out of 721 nights together between April 2011 and March 2013. There were also 100 events scheduled for “family time.”
But a lawyer for Mr. McDonnell argued how little such data might reveal about a marriage. On nights that Mr. McDonnell slept in the Governor’s Mansion, he sometimes did not return there until midnight. On at least a couple of those evenings when the governor was working late, mansion logs showed Mr. Williams visited after 6 p.m. to see “102,” police code for the first lady. Driving home the point that a couple might not be harmonious just because they are under the same roof, the defense lawyer, John Brownlee, reprised a wrenching email Mr. McDonnell had read in court, dated Sept. 5, 2011 — when the couple were home together — in which he told his wife,  “I am so spiritually and mentally exhausted,” from marital strife.

Israel
and Ismail Haniya, the

-based political leader of
Hamas

while Hamas, the Islamist
Palestinian
faction that dominates

In Gaza, banks reopened, markets were crowded, bulldozers began to remove rubble blocking roads and fishermen ventured out to sea, seizing on the cease-fire deal’s return of the zone permitted by Israel to six nautical miles, as agreed in 2012, from three nautical miles since June. “Turn” could mean a lot of things. The Turn is what survivors on “The Walking Dead” call their zombie apocalypse. Repeated three times, it’s the title of a folk song, and it’s the first half of turncoat, as in traitor, or turndown, as in turndown service in a fancy hotel, or maybe just turnip, the root vegetable.
It’s also the name of
a new AMC drama
starting Sunday about espionage during the Revolutionary War, and refers to the act of “turning” a person to the cause. And the somewhat elliptical title is oddly apt, a tip-off of obscurity yet to come.
This series is ambitious and beautifully filmed. The story, based on the book “Washington’s Spies” by Alexander Rose, is inherently intriguing: a look at real-life anti-British conspirators known as the Culper Ring, a few men — and women — who risked their lives to give Gen. George Washington advance word about enemy movements.
Once the ring gets going and the espionage kicks in, the story becomes clear and exciting. The battle scenes are disturbingly vivid, and most of the characters are interesting right off the bat: not all redcoats are alike, and the Continental Army has its own share of opportunists, cowards and war criminals.
But the premiere episode assumes that viewers are so familiar with the period and this more obscure chapter of history that the main characters’ allegiances, motives, and struggles will be clear from the outset. They are not.
Nathan Hale, the American agent who famously regretted not having more than one life to give for his country, is not seen in this account.
The action begins in the fall of 1776 with a lesser-known, real-life hero, Abraham Woodhull, a young cabbage farmer in Setauket, on the North Shore of Long Island. It’s not immediately obvious that Abraham is the hero, because, no doubt commendably, the creators cast a British actor (Jamie Bell), who doesn’t look heroic or even classically handsome — he is slight, pale and has a sharp, almost rodentlike face.
Abraham speaks with a slight Irish lilt, which is supposed to signal his unconscious resistance to the British occupation (no one hates the English better than the Irish). But that’s a bit confusing at first, particularly because his Tory father, Judge Richard Woodhull (Kevin R. McNally), speaks with a flat American accent with some English inflection.
Abraham has a wife, Mary (Meegan Warner), and a baby, but he hasn’t gotten over his first love, Anna Strong (Heather Lind), who is married to a tavernkeeper and not so secretly supports the anti-British rebels who call themselves the Patriots.
Washington’s army is in flight, and the British occupy New York City and Long Island. British soldiers are all over Setauket, particularly the tavern, and Abraham and Mary have a soldier billeted at their farmhouse. Abraham is not a loyalist like his father, but he doesn’t want any trouble. “If one redcoat in the house is as close as it comes to us,” he tells Mary, “then I shall thank the Lord and be done with it.”
But it proves impossible to stay neutral or safe. Abraham gets pulled to the side of the Patriots, more for personal reasons than principle. He wants to protect Anna from the slimy overtures of Captain Simcoe (Samuel Roukin). He is also being leaned on very heavily by a childhood friend, Ben Tallmadge (Seth Numrich), a Yale classmate of Hale’s who, like Hale, joined Washington’s army.
The 18th-century spycraft is fun — signals are sent by the color and alignment of petticoats waving on a clothesline. But sometimes the creators’ quest for authenticity is so ardent that it makes the story hard to follow: when spies grope around in the dark, the screen is so black that it’s difficult to detect who is saying what.
“Turn” doesn’t dumb down history for the audience. Instead, it gives life to some of the messier parts of a period that is too often starched and oversimplified by schoolbooks and politicians. “Turn” isn’t easy, but then again, neither was the American Revolution.

I thought I could hold it together, that if I was broadcasting crazy it was at least in a glamorous silent-film-star kind of way. Perfect eyeliner surrounding a glint of madness. But obviously I wasn’t pulling it off. A friend intervened: “You’re freaking me out. I’m going to take you to a woman who has helped me out of tough times before.” She set up the appointment and I washed up at her tarot card reader’s Manhattan apartment.
As an intellectual or whatever, I was skeptical. I was worried it was going to be one of those “You’ll meet a handsome man in the next six weeks” kind of deals. I was also worried that I was desperate enough to latch on to such empty platitudes.
She laid out the cards in a cross and tower as we made small talk. I could see a number of knights, a woman weeping, a man hanging upside down from a tree. She laid a finger on the woman. “You’re in distress?”
Oh God, yes. Not that she needed a card to tell her that. I was not sleeping, I felt eaten alive by anxiety. I started talking: not enough money, my family is a nightmare, my love life is a disaster… She stopped me. “It’s like you’re drowning in a birdbath. Stand up, it’s just a birdbath.”
She showed me the cards again, and what had at first looked to me like a representation of despair now didn’t seem so bad. The knights were in battle mode, yes, but the cards around them were harmless little twos and threes. They were fighting what looked like a guy juggling coins and three women dancing around with cups. Even that hanged man had a look of serenity on his face. Her cat, a beautiful Egyptian Mau, butted her head against my legs and I took a look around the apartment. Her bookshelves were not stocked with hokey books about angels or Gypsies; they were filled with psychological texts, Byzantine histories, gorgeous art books. Her furniture was minimalist and refined. The only hint at her day job was a painting of what is traditionally the first card of the tarot, the embodiment of joy and fearlessness: the fool.
Her reading taught me two things: With a change of strategy, I could get back in control of my life and, also, I wanted to learn how to do this.
Within days, I had bought my own deck of tarot cards. It came with a flimsy manual full of lines like “The queen of coins is an older woman in your life, Virgo, Taurus or Capricorn.” I binged and bought half a dozen books, guides to the meaning of the cards and the different spreads.
I was immediately disappointed. The problem is that I am a book critic. It is no longer possible for me to read a text without taking it apart in my head. And if you take apart one of these tarot books, you’ll be left with nothing. Some soggy material full of mystical woo-woo language and soft ideas about karma and the spirit realm. Or self-help clichés, “no one will love you until you learn to love yourself” nonsense. The writers seemed incapable of distilling the experience I had had, and instead just wanted to tell me how to foretell the future or figure out why that guy left me.
I didn’t believe that the tarot cards were a way of the gods getting messages across (they can use Facebook, like everyone else). And I didn’t want to repair my psyche — I was unconvinced that it was broken. Reading books about tarot made me want to abandon my tarot endeavor altogether.
But I kept coming back to the power of that reading. What she was really doing was telling me a story about my life.
We all tell ourselves stories, as a way to understand and cope with what’s happening. But this one was different from what I had been telling myself, that I lost that job because I was stupid, that he had left because I was unworthy of love, that I was the brave victim of circumstance. The cards — those crossed and reversed and strangely placed knights — weren’t disciplined fighters, they were bringers of chaos. I saw that I had been picking fights against everything in my life because I was dissatisfied. Then there was the nine of swords — the weapons stacked one atop another above a woman with her head in her hands — which was the ultimate “I am going to lie here in despair, just step over me it’s fine” card. It wasn’t a story I wanted to hear. But it showed me how to make changes.
Sometimes you think you’re valiantly battling a dragon, but really you’re drowning in a birdbath.
Stories were my way in. Those figures in the cards became characters and plot points. I would pull one card every morning, and then look for that character or that plot point in my own life. That argument I keep having with my ex, the one that never resolves? Five of swords. That one-way plane ticket to Berlin? The world. Slowly, over a period of eight years, I began to understand the patterns and how to put the narrative together.
I was still terrified to come out as a tarot reader. If you want to lose respect in the intellectual realm, start banging on about Mercury retrogrades or someone’s aura. But after dinner with friends, I would haltingly start talking about what I’ve been spending so much of my time on. The husbands would roll their eyes. The wives would want readings of their own. Eventually, I began to offer my own services as a reader. Cringingly at first, I put up a notice. Tarot card readings: no prognostication or velvet muumuus, guaranteed!
What if I couldn’t find the thread of the story? I stumbled through the first several readings. But then a woman came to me, flush from an affair. She wanted to talk about her new lover and how great it all was. I laid out the cards. The hierophant — a figure of holy wisdom — reversed. The king of swords, crossing the lovers. My client was represented by the grumbling, tyrannical emperor. I could see what the story was, but it wasn’t the happy one she had just told me. “This isn’t about your new lover,” I told her, and I could see her glow fade. “We have to talk about the marriage you are betraying.” It was a difficult, but valuable, conversation.
Now writers, housewives, doctors, carpenters, a whole variety of people come to me. They tell me the source of their distress or ask me their question. And I take out my cards and I tell them a story.

Bookslut
.

Stained Glass Window
Daniel Finkel
Can an itinerant pilgrim find a four-sided shape (besides the blue diamond) that touches each side of the grid at one of the numbered points and takes up exactly half the area of the original 16-box grid?
One-Round War
Stern and Mackenzie
It’s war. In what order should you play your cards in order to maximize the chances of having the highest card as you and your opponent turn over cards in succession?
More Monster and Hats
Chris Roat
A monster puts a black or white hat on two people’s heads and has them face each other. They then simultaneously announce the color of the hat they are wearing. If at least one person is correct, the pair will be set free. What should they do?
The Princess Problem
Dave Penneys
A princess lives in a row of adjacent connected rooms, which also have doors to the outside. The princess never stays in the same room two days in a row. How can a suitor find her if allowed one knock per day?
Hidato
Gyora Benedek
Find the Path… Solve the Puzzle: Find the missing numbers between one and the largest so that consecutive numbers touch. Hidato puzzles have unique solutions and can be solved by logic only: no trial and error required.
The Necktie Paradox
Greg Ross
Two men agree to a wager: whoever is wearing the most expensive tie has to give it to the other. Each thinks they have a 50% chance of winning a more valuable tie, meaning the wager would have a positive expected value for each of the men. How can this be?
Randomness Game
Humble and Nishiyama
A variation on the classic Penney’s Game using a deck of cards. Can you determine a winning strategy?
Dinner Rolls
Giovanni Ciriani
A baker offers a reasonable number of free rolls before charging a fee. Two customers eat 12 rolls and are charged $4. If one person had eaten the rolls, the charge would have been $14. How many roles may one person eat for free?
The Devil’s Penny
Henk Tijms
Eleven closed boxes with known sums of money are mixed up and placed in front of you. You may open boxes and keep the contents unless you open the box with a Devil’s penny. Then you lose everything you’ve gained. What should you do?
The Pi Machine
Alon Amit
Put one ball near a wall and roll another toward it. The first ball will hit the one near the wall, which will bounce off the wall and come back to hit the first ball. Three collisions. The first digit of pi is a three. How can this work? (Original research by Gregory Galperin.)
A Coin Problem
Daniel Finkel
Design a game, using only a fair coin, that you have a 1/3 chance of winning.
A Large Urn
Hirokazu Iwasawa
Draw from an urn containing 600 black and 400 white marbles until you have removed all marbles of one of the colors. What is the probability that at least one white marble will be left in the urn?
Magic Square
Ethan Brown
Complete a 4 x 4 magic square with the values 2, 11 and 5 placed as shown so that each row, each column and each diagonal sums to 79.
Mental Math
Art Benjamin
Are you a fan of mental arithmetic? How might you do the following in your head: 96 × 96, 46 × 42, 81 × 59, 89 × 72 and 13
3
?
Rectangle Puzzle
Sol Golomb
Create a set of five rectangles that have sides of length 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 10 units. How many different sets of five rectangles are possible?
Tricky Dice
Joshua Zucker
Design three dice (each with three distinct numbers between one and nine, with opposing faces identical) so that no matter which die your opponent chooses, you’ll always be able to choose a better die.
N U M + B E R = P L A Y
Bill Gosper
For the expression
N U M + B E R = P L A Y,
which distinct numerals (each different) can be substituted for letters to make a valid expression? How many solutions are there?
Hopscotch Loops
Daniel Finkel
Label four squares as shown above. Starting at the first square, you could hop 2 squares to 1, 1 square to 3, and 3 squares back to 2, landing on all squares but zero. How many many squares can you string together to successfully play this game?
KenKen®
Tetsuya Miyamoto
Fill in the whole grid of numbers to fulfill the rules indicated in the cages, making sure no number is repeated in any grid or column.
The Primo Puzzle
Finkel and Cook
Try Primo, the new prime number-based board game by the Math for Love duo Daniel Finkel and Katherine Cook.
Crunched Charms
Dave Auckly
An introduction to knot theory by Dave Auckly. Can you restore the above shapes to their original symmetric forms?
The 403 Match Puzzle
Paulo Ferro
The number 403 above is created out of 15 matches. Modify the position of two matches to obtain a number divisible by 9. How many solutions are there? Find them!
Ping-Pong Redux
Bennett and Pickford
Dan and Avery reduce their ping-pong score by dividing by a common factor when possible: An 8-4 score would become 2-1. What are all possible final scores?
Sicherman’s Dice
George Sicherman
How can two 6-sided cubes be numbered in order to produce totals indistinguishable from those produced by a standard pair of dice?
The Apple Conundrum
Greg Ross
Two women are selling apples. The first sells 30 apples at 2 for $1, earning $15. The second sells 30 apples at 3 for $1, earning $10. Between them they’ve sold 60 apples for $25. What became of the other dollar?
World Cup Group Play
Marco Moriconi
In the World Cup group play round, each of four teams plays each other once. A team scores 3 points for a win, 1 point for a draw (tie) and 0 for a loss. How many different possible final point standings are possible?
Penalty Kick Shootout
Marco Moriconi
Two soccer teams. The better team scores 80 percent of its penalty kicks, and the other team scores 70 percent. If the teams are tied after the penalty kick shootout, what are the odds the better team will win the sudden death stage?
Straights and Flushes
Bram Cohen
Take a deck of cards and turn over one at a time, noting the best possible five-card hand that can be created by any five of the cards you’ve turned over. Which would you expect to see first — a straight or a flush?
Twelve-Coin Problem
Stephan Peers
You have 12 coins that all look exactly the same. One is counterfeit and is either heavier or lighter than the other 11. With a balance beam scale, isolate the counterfeit coin in three moves.
Path Puzzles
Roderick Kimball
Use the guide numbers outside the grid to create a single path from entrance to exit, as you would a maze.
At the Video Store
Joe Fendel
While at the video store I choose 5 movies. One child eliminates 2 options, narrowing the field to 3. The other child then eliminates 2 more options. If you were one of the children, which step would you choose?
Flying Squirrel
Daniel Finkel
A flying squirrel-frog is being chased by two cats. In which starting configurations will the cats catch the flying squirrel-frog? In which configurations will the flying squirrel-frog escape?
Ariadne’s String
Gordon Hamilton
Theseus ties a string through a room of columns, always increasing the distance between columns he touches. How many straight-line segments can Theseus create?
Two Cookies Puzzle
(Classic)
Toll-collecting trolls take half the cookies you are carrying over a series of five bridges, giving one cookie back each time. How many cookies will you need to end up with two?
Ants on a Triangle
Peter Norvig
There are three ants on a triangle, one at each corner. Suddenly they each start walking along an edge of the triangle. What is the probability that the ants don’t collide?
Bugs on a Square
Cem Ünsal
Four bugs at the corners of a square; each moves toward its neighbor. How far does a bug travel before reaching it?
Bullfrog Puzzle
Vinegar and Cosman
An androgynous frog species mates in a peculiar way. Can you predict what will happen when you connect multiple families?
Train Puzzle
Gary Hewitt
Gary Hewitt lives halfway between two train stations. If he wants to get to work as quickly as possible, does it matter which station he walks to?
Light in a Big Room
Hansen Chen
How could you wire a number of simple analogue switches to operate a chandelier in the middle of a big bedroom?
Icosian Game
Pádraig Kirwan
A challenge conceived by Sir William Hamilton, the Irish mathematician.
Find a path that passes through all the vertices only once, and then returns to the starting point.
Three-Card Swindle
Susan Holmes
A banker shakes three cards in a hat and lets you pick one and put it on the table. He then bets even money that the underside suit is the same as the top. Is this fair? (From Martin Gardner’s Aha! Gotcha.)
The Cube Clock
Scott Kim
A calendar displays the date using two cubes. What are the four digits that cannot be seen on the left cube and the three that cannot be seen on the right cube? (First popularized by Martin Gardner.)
Not Breaking the Duck
Ian Stewart
A post celebrating Martin Gardner’s centennial featuring an object-find challenge by Lucian McLellan and a duck egg puzzle by Ian Stewart.
The Circle-Toss Game
Daniel Finkel
A group of kids form a circle, throwing a ball to the left to an increasingly large number of people. If each person touches the ball before it gets back to the first person, how many kids are in the circle?
Truth-Tellers and Liars
Marco Moriconi
The first in a line of truth-tellers and liars sings, “There’s at least one liar here!”, the second one goes, “There are at least two liars here!” and so on, until the end of the line. Who is lying? Who is telling the truth?
Navajo Sheep
Dave Auckly
Divide each strand of colored sheep to give the Black Sheep Clan exactly half black sheep, the Mud Clan exactly half brown sheep, and Water’s Edge exactly half white sheep.
Hemlock Soames
Ian Stewart
Can you complete this clueless pseudoku from Professor Stewart’s
Casebook of Mathematical Mysteries
?
Making Way
Greg Ross
A train approaches a man 4/7 of the way across a trestle. The man can run toward the train or away, barely reaching safety either way. If he runs at 15 miles an hour, how fast is the train going?
Path Puzzles
Roderick Kimball
Use guide numbers outside the grid to find your way from entrance to exit.
Bike Path
George Hart
A bicycle leaves tracks as it passes through snow (or mud). How can you tell which way the bicycle was traveling by the shape of the tracks?
The Doctor’s Dilemma
Ed Fredkin
A doctor possesses an unusual ability to heal through touch. What should she do?
